section_summary: This section centers on Kilsoo K. Haan and the Sino-Korean Peoples League's warnings about Japanese political, cultural, and military influence in Hawaii. A substantial group of records concerns the unsuccessful effort in Haan's libel suit against the Nippu Jiji Company to obtain depositions from Japanese diplomats and former consular officials in Brazil, Argentina, South Africa, and Japan; State Department officials concluded that diplomatic immunity, foreign law, and international-relations concerns made execution of the commissions improper. The section also contains two copies or versions of Haan's polemic “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii,” correspondence submitting it to the Roosevelt administration and Congress, and naval-intelligence translations concerning Japanese consular surveillance and organization of Japanese communities in Hawaii.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting confidential reports on Anglo-Japanese negotiations and the Shanghai International Settlement
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples League
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Haan reports rumors of proposed Anglo-Japanese understandings and a prospective reign of terror in the Shanghai International Settlement.
subfiles.summary: Haan forwards purported confidential information that Britain had encouraged Japan to approach Neville Chamberlain about restoring an Anglo-Japanese understanding. The reported terms included Japanese nonaggression toward the Dutch East Indies, Australia, and India, British recognition of Japan's paramount interests in China, joint development in South China, and British neutrality in a Japanese-Soviet conflict. Haan also reports rumors of September violence in the Shanghai International Settlement while disclaiming certainty about his sources.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 403: Commission to Take Testimony of the Japanese Minister to the Union of South Africa
subfiles.from: H. Earle Russell, American Consul General, Johannesburg
subfiles.to: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Russell explains why he believes the court commission seeking Kanekazu Okada's testimony cannot properly be executed.
subfiles.summary: Russell forwards Hawaiian court papers from Kilsoo Haan's libel suit and notes that Okada, then the Japanese minister to South Africa, was temporarily in Cape Town rather than Pretoria. He argues that the commission does not authorize the Cape Town consulate to act and that approaching a foreign diplomatic representative would be improper. The interrogatories appear to concern an alleged racial and political plot in Hawaii, making refusal likely even apart from Okada's official status.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding commission and interrogatories in Kil Son Hahn v. Nippu Jiji Co.
subfiles.from: Arthur E. Restarick, Chief Clerk, First Circuit Court of Hawaii
subfiles.to: United States Consul General, Pretoria
subfiles.about: The Hawaiian court clerk asks the consul general to arrange Kanekazu Okada's deposition.
subfiles.summary: Restarick encloses a certified court order, an original commission, and proposed direct interrogatories in the Haan–Nippu Jiji libel case. He identifies Okada's Pretoria legation address and asks that the deposition be taken and the original papers returned according to the commission's directions.

subfiles.title: Order for Commission to Take Deposition, Law No. 15,541
subfiles.from: Circuit Court of the First Judicial Circuit, Territory of Hawaii
subfiles.to: Designated United States consular officers abroad
subfiles.about: The court orders commissions for the examination of nine overseas witnesses in Kilsoo Haan's libel suit.
subfiles.summary: The order grants the defendant's request to examine nine witnesses outside Hawaii by written interrogatories, with Haan's attorney consenting and waiving cross-interrogatories. It prescribes the oath, transcription, signature, certification, return, filing, and later use of the depositions at trial.

subfiles.title: Commission to Take Depositions, Law No. 15,541
subfiles.from: Circuit Court of the First Judicial Circuit, Territory of Hawaii
subfiles.to: United States consular officers in Rio de Janeiro, Tokyo, Pretoria, and Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: The commission authorizes American consular officers to depose nine witnesses abroad in the Haan–Nippu Jiji case.
subfiles.summary: The court states that the witnesses are material and cannot personally attend the Hawaiian proceeding. Consular officers in four countries are directed to administer oaths, record and obtain signatures on answers, certify the testimony, and return the materials under seal to Honolulu.

subfiles.title: Proposed Direct Interrogatories to Overseas Witnesses
subfiles.from: Nippu Jiji Company, Limited, through the First Circuit Court of Hawaii
subfiles.to: Nine proposed witnesses, including former Japanese consular officials
subfiles.about: The questions seek testimony about alleged meetings to unite Asians in Hawaii against the white population.
subfiles.summary: The interrogatories ask each witness's identity, occupation, Hawaii residence, and acquaintance with Kilsoo Haan. They then ask about a supposed movement among Asians to combine against or expel Hawaii's white population and whether relevant meetings occurred at the Japanese consulate. The final question asks whether a consul general or acting consul general would have known of such meetings.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 407: Commission to Take Testimony of the Japanese Consul
subfiles.from: Monnett B. Davis, American Consul General, Buenos Aires
subfiles.to: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Davis requests instructions concerning a commission to depose Japanese consul Toyokichi Fukuma.
subfiles.summary: Davis submits the Hawaiian commission and interrogatories directed to Toyokichi Fukuma, the Japanese consul in Buenos Aires. Because Fukuma represented a foreign government and the questions implicated international relations, Davis considers execution inadvisable and asks the Department for instructions.

subfiles.title: Copy of Commission to Take Depositions enclosed with Despatch No. 407
subfiles.from: Circuit Court of the First Judicial Circuit, Territory of Hawaii
subfiles.to: United States consular officers in Rio de Janeiro, Tokyo, Pretoria, and Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: This enclosure reproduces the court's authorization to examine nine witnesses outside Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The commission identifies the witnesses as material to Kilsoo Haan's suit against Nippu Jiji and authorizes their examination by written interrogatories. It provides detailed instructions for sworn answers, signatures, certification, sealing, and return to the court in Honolulu.

subfiles.title: Copy of Proposed Direct Interrogatories enclosed with Despatch No. 407
subfiles.from: Nippu Jiji Company, Limited, through the First Circuit Court of Hawaii
subfiles.to: Nine proposed witnesses
subfiles.about: The enclosure asks former Hawaii residents and officials about an alleged Asian movement against Hawaii's white population.
subfiles.summary: The questions cover the witnesses' occupation, residence in Hawaii, and acquaintance with Kilsoo Haan. They probe alleged meetings at the Japanese consulate or elsewhere to organize Asians against the white population and ask whether consular officials would have known of any such meeting.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on disposition of the Rio de Janeiro commission
subfiles.from: Division of Foreign Service Administration
subfiles.to: Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: The memorandum suggests that no instruction is needed concerning Rio de Janeiro's unexecuted deposition commission.
subfiles.summary: The writer notes that the Rio consul general cannot execute the commission and that the Department has no apparent need to examine it. Because the Hawaiian court may not want it returned, the memorandum proposes taking no further action and requests concurrence.

subfiles.title: Memorandum and routing endorsements on Despatch No. 403
subfiles.from: Office of an Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: George S. Messersmith and reviewing divisions
subfiles.about: The memorandum circulates the Johannesburg despatch for legal, regional, and possible Interior Department review.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum asks whether the Johannesburg consul general acted correctly in declining to seek testimony from the Japanese minister to South Africa. It emphasizes the highly sensitive questions and proposes review by the European, Far Eastern, and Legal divisions, with possible notice to the Interior Department because the litigation arose in Hawaii. Routing endorsements continue on page 345.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum concurring against execution of the commissions
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: State Department reviewing officials
subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs explains why Japanese officials and witnesses were unlikely or legally unable to testify through American consulates.
subfiles.summary: The division concurs with the American Republics division and doubts that the Japanese consul general in Buenos Aires or the other proposed witnesses would testify voluntarily. It states that Japanese law prohibited American diplomatic or consular offices from taking testimony in Japan. The memorandum also identifies Haan as a Korean, a Japanese subject, and the Washington representative of the Sino-Korean Peoples League.

subfiles.title: American Republics memorandum on Despatch No. 407
subfiles.from: Laurence Duggan, Division of the American Republics
subfiles.to: Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: Duggan recommends against executing the Buenos Aires commission and requests a legal opinion.
subfiles.summary: The division considers it poor policy to have an American consul question a Japanese consul about matters affecting Japanese-American relations. Duggan asks whether the Hawaiian commission is legally mandatory and recommends uniform instructions to Buenos Aires, Rio de Janeiro, Tokyo, and Pretoria after a decision is reached.

subfiles.title: Foreign Service Administration memorandum requesting guidance on the Buenos Aires despatch
subfiles.from: Division of Foreign Service Administration
subfiles.to: Divisions of the American Republics, Far Eastern Affairs, European Affairs, and the Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: The memorandum circulates the Buenos Aires request because of the confidential and legal character of the proposed testimony.
subfiles.summary: The originating office asks whether the regional divisions wish to answer the consul general or recommend a reply. A handwritten response characterizes the issue as principally legal, notes the Japanese consul's official status and possible Argentine-law concerns, and suggests avoiding execution if possible.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser memorandum on authority to execute foreign deposition commissions
subfiles.from: Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.to: State Department regional and administrative divisions
subfiles.about: The Legal Adviser concludes that American consuls are not required to execute the Hawaiian commission.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that consular officers may take testimony abroad only when permitted by local law or practice. Japan required letters rogatory through diplomatic channels, while the Japanese minister in South Africa was immune from judicial process. Execution in Argentina or Brazil was considered highly improbable, and the Department was assumed to oppose action there.

subfiles.title: Copy of Legal Adviser memorandum on foreign deposition commissions
subfiles.from: Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.to: State Department regional and administrative divisions
subfiles.about: This copy restates the legal conclusion that American consular officers need not execute the commissions.
subfiles.summary: The document explains that consular execution depends upon the law and practice of the country concerned. It rules out action in Japan without diplomatic letters rogatory and in South Africa because the proposed witness was an immune Japanese minister. It also regards execution in Buenos Aires or Rio de Janeiro as highly improbable.

subfiles.title: Letter to the First Circuit Court clerk declining consular execution
subfiles.from: Nathaniel P. Davis, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Clerk, Circuit Court, First Judicial Circuit, Honolulu
subfiles.about: The State Department informs the Hawaiian court that its overseas deposition commissions cannot appropriately be executed.
subfiles.summary: The Department reviews the commissions sent to Rio de Janeiro, Tokyo, Pretoria, and Buenos Aires and identifies Fukuma and Okada as Japanese officials. It explains that testimony in Japan required letters rogatory and that Japanese government representatives elsewhere could not properly be pressed to answer questions concerning official activities. The clerk is therefore advised that American consular officers should take no action toward execution.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American consular officer at Johannesburg
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Johannesburg
subfiles.about: The Department transmits its letter to the Hawaiian court for information and guidance.
subfiles.summary: The instruction acknowledges receipt of the original commission in the Haan–Nippu Jiji case. It encloses the Department's response to the Hawaiian clerk and notes that similar instructions were sent to Rio de Janeiro, Buenos Aires, and Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American consular officer at Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: The Department provides guidance against acting on the Hawaiian deposition commission.
subfiles.summary: The instruction summarizes the commissions received in Buenos Aires and Johannesburg and their requests for testimony from Japanese officials. A copy of the Department's letter to the Hawaiian court clerk is enclosed as guidance, with notice that equivalent instructions went to the other affected posts.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American consular officer at Buenos Aires
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: The Department answers Despatch No. 407 by enclosing its response to the Hawaiian court.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges the Buenos Aires despatch concerning the Haan–Nippu Jiji deposition commission. It sends its letter to the court clerk for the post's guidance and reports that similar instructions were issued to Rio de Janeiro, Johannesburg, and Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American consular officer at Tokyo
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department advises the Tokyo post of its handling of the Hawaiian deposition commissions.
subfiles.summary: The instruction describes the commissions reported by Buenos Aires and Johannesburg and the official status of Fukuma and Okada. It encloses the Department's letter to the Hawaiian court and notes parallel instructions to the other affected consular posts.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 612: Commission to Take Deposition of Japanese Ambassador to Brazil
subfiles.from: William C. Burdett, American Consul General, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.to: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Burdett reports that his office did not approach Japanese ambassador Kazue Kuwashima and will retain the commission unless instructed otherwise.
subfiles.summary: The Rio consulate received a commission similar to those discussed in the Department's June 16 instruction. It refrained from approaching the Japanese ambassador and drafted, but did not mail, a response to the Hawaiian court. Burdett proposes retaining the papers unless the Department wants them submitted or returned.

subfiles.title: Draft letter returning the commission concerning Kazue Kuwashima
subfiles.from: American Consulate General, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.to: Arthur E. Restarick, Chief Clerk, First Circuit Court of Hawaii
subfiles.about: The unmailed draft explains that diplomatic immunity prevents examination of the Japanese ambassador to Brazil.
subfiles.summary: The draft identifies Kuwashima as the Japanese ambassador and states that he cannot testify in foreign litigation without his government's express consent. It also finds some interrogatories objectionable because they concern matters protected by his official character. The draft would have returned the commission and interrogatories.

subfiles.title: Letter submitting “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to the White House
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.to: Stephen Early, Secretary to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Haan asks Early to read his article and bring its anti-Japanization proposals to President Roosevelt's attention.
subfiles.summary: Haan encloses an article written in 1936 and recently revised, arguing that Japan's penetration extends to Hawaii and the American Pacific Coast. He renews requests for presidential sympathy toward Korea, an embargo on essential war materials to Japan, and permission for Korean students in America to remain and counter Japanese activities.

subfiles.title: “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii”
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.to: President Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Haan argues that Japanese political, cultural, economic, and military influence in Hawaii threatens American security.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet portrays Japan as pursuing racial equality and world power through territorial expansion, Pacific island bases, fishing fleets, consular influence, and organizations among overseas Japanese. It reviews nineteenth-century Japanese pressure on Hawaii and criticizes the Prince Fushimi scholarship fund, Japanese Christianity, dual nationality practices, and Japanese language schools as instruments of Japanization. Haan predicts possible conflict in the Pacific and urges an embargo on war materials plus moral support for China and Korea. Its claims combine historical narrative, quotations, demographic figures, and warnings about Hawaii's military vulnerability.

subfiles.title: Office of Naval Intelligence memorandum forwarding Hawaiian press material
subfiles.from: E. B. Nixon, Commander, U.S. Navy
subfiles.to: Fletcher Warren, Department of State
subfiles.about: Nixon forwards press translations concerning Japanese organizations and consular activity in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The brief memorandum sends an enclosure to the State Department because it may be of interest. The accompanying pages summarize Japanese-language press reports about coordination of overseas Japanese communities and Hawaiian consular surveys.

subfiles.title: Translations and summaries of Hawaiian Japanese-language newspaper reports
subfiles.from: Office of Naval Intelligence compilation from Hawaii Hochi, Hawaii Mainichi, Maui Shimbun, Kauai Shimpo, and Nippu Jiji
subfiles.to: Department of State
subfiles.about: The digest reports Japanese government and consular efforts to organize, survey, and coordinate Japanese communities in Hawaii and abroad.
subfiles.summary: A March article describes a Tokyo organization intended to coordinate overseas Japanese, their newspapers, propaganda, immigration matters, and second-generation issues. May reports describe Honolulu consular requests for comprehensive inventories of Japanese civic, religious, commercial, educational, and social bodies in Hilo and Maui. Further items recount Vice-Consul Toshijiro Kudo's consultations with consular agents across Kauaʻi and the Hilo Japanese Society's division of the survey work.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Commander Nixon's memorandum
subfiles.from: Department of State on behalf of Fletcher Warren
subfiles.to: Commander E. B. Nixon
subfiles.about: The State Department acknowledges receipt of the naval-intelligence memorandum and enclosure.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum records Warren's acknowledgment of Nixon's July 12 forwarding of material considered of interest to the Department of State.

subfiles.title: Letter submitting “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to Francis B. Sayre
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.to: Francis B. Sayre, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Haan sends Sayre his article and urges a positive American policy against Japanese expansion and influence.
subfiles.summary: Haan notes that the article had also been presented to Senate foreign-relations, naval, and military committees. He describes Japanese aggression as a threat to Pacific peace and as penetration of the Western sphere of influence. The letter frames the submission as an appeal for international harmony and a stronger American response.

subfiles.title: Letter submitting “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to Senate committees
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples League of Hawaii
subfiles.to: Members of the Senate Foreign Relations, Naval, and Military Committees
subfiles.about: Haan asks senators to consider Hawaii's and Guam's strategic vulnerability to Japanese domination.
subfiles.summary: Haan submits his article in view of crises in the Far East and stresses Hawaii's strategic importance. Citing Laura Thompson's Guam research, he says Guamanians fear Japanese rule and desire American fortification. He compares the danger to Korea's loss of independence and hopes Guam and Hawaii will avoid Korea's fate.

subfiles.title: “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii,” congressional version or reprint
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.to: United States Senate committees
subfiles.about: This second version repeats Haan's argument that Japanese expansion and Japanization endanger Hawaii and American Pacific power.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion includes the preface, contents, and opening discussions of Japan's national mission, Pacific territorial strategy, possible attack on Hawaii, and earlier diplomatic pressure on the Hawaiian government. It also begins sections on “duck diplomacy” and racial relations in Hawaii. Pages 390–391 and 392–393 contain partly duplicated text, and the pamphlet continues beyond the end of this supplied section.
